source.title: Live: Learning Video LLM with Streaming Speech Transcription at Scale
source.authors: Joya Chen; Zi-Yun Zeng; Yiqi Lin; Yi-Qi Lin; Wei Li; Ze-Jun Ma; M. Shou

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how downstream task scores change with pretraining data scale, using video commentary and QA metrics rather than held-out cross-entropy loss or the original language-model scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: Table 1c reports a pretraining-data-size sweep and downstream scores. The study does not report held-out cross-entropy scaling, parameter- or compute-scaling sweeps, extrapolation from small runs, or architecture-shape effects. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited, but their scaling laws are not tested here.
record.test_reason: Table 1c varies pretraining data (1M–10M clips) for one 7B video LLM and reports downstream scores. This bears on V6 (downstream gains with data scale) in a new setting, video-ASR streaming pretraining. No loss, parameter or compute sweeps are reported, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say commentary consistently improves with more pretraining data, while QA declines beyond 5M, likely because the pretraining data is single-source (streaming ASR).
record.recipe_differences: This is a video-LLM pretraining data-size ablation evaluated on downstream tasks, not the original language-model held-out-loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with data size and evaluation task: commentary improves through 10M clips, whereas Video-MME overall and short-video scores peak at 5M and decline at 10M.
record.problems: The relevant sweep varies data size for one 7B model and uses shortened 30–60s clips; it reports downstream task metrics rather than held-out loss. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were included: the other ablations change training paradigm or context, while the remaining tables compare models or report task performance without a pretraining-scale sweep (Table 1a–b, Tables 2–4).

untested.parts: Predictability (no fitted trend or extrapolation); parameter or compute scaling; performance as a function of pretraining loss; medium and long Video-MME videos; multiple seeds.
No held-out loss reported against parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger runs.
Video-domain loss scaling form not measured; only downstream scores at four data sizes.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The data-size sweep is confounded with data quality. Subsets are formed by ranking clips by word-set size, so larger subsets add less informative clips. The ablation uses 30–60s clips and 120 frames, a single run per point, and no uncertainty estimates. Whether training epochs or compute were held constant across sizes is not stated. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as motivation. This is a weak, four-point downstream test of V6 in a video-LLM setting.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation comparison or parameter/token allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study uses video models, but does not test whether power-law loss scaling holds in video or other modalities or training regimes.
Tests only data-size scaling for one 7B video-model setup on commentary and video QA; does not test parameter scaling or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or loss-curve bending.

relationships.condition: LiveSports-3K-CC commentary win rate, 1M–10M clips, LiveCC-7B-Base ablation
relationships.reason: Win rate rises at every data step, 29.1→30.8→32.9→36.0 (r1–r4). No fit is given, so only monotonic improvement is shown.
relationships.display_finding: Win rate increased at every data step from 29.1 to 30.8 to 32.9 to 36.0.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: LiveSports-3K-CC commentary win rate, 1M–10M clips, LiveCC-7B-Base ablation
source_check.reason: Table 1c confirms monotonic commentary gains of 29.1, 30.8, 32.9 and 36.0 across r1–r4. This supports improvement within the tested range; predictive fitting is untested.

relationships.condition: Video-MME overall and short-video scores, 1M–5M clips
relationships.reason: QA gains are small: overall rises only 0.4 (r5–r7) and short-video 2.0 (r9–r11), with no uncertainty. The improvement is much weaker than for commentary.
relationships.display_finding: Overall scores increased by only 0.4 points and short-video scores by 2.0, much less than commentary gains, without reported uncertainty.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Video-MME overall and short-video scores, 1M–5M clips
source_check.reason: Across r5–r7 and r9–r11, overall improves only 60.6→61.0 and short-video 68.1→70.1. These small gains qualify the strength of downstream improvement under the supplied state rules.

relationships.condition: Video-MME overall and short-video scores, 10M vs 5M clips
relationships.reason: Both QA scores fall at 10M (61.0→58.0 in r8; 70.1→67.6 in r12). The authors attribute this to single-source data, not to scale itself.
relationships.display_finding: Overall and short-video QA scores fell from 61.0 to 58.0 and 70.1 to 67.6, respectively, which the authors attributed to single-source data.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Video-MME overall and short-video scores, 10M vs 5M clips
source_check.reason: Table 1c confirms reversals: overall 61.0→58.0 and short-video 70.1→67.6 in r8 and r12. Section 5.2 explicitly reports declining QA beyond 5M.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
